Warm Springs

Warm Springs can name a constituent people as well as the contemporary confederated government that includes Wasco and Paiute people. These readings keep those histories visible while introducing language education, museum work and selected 1855 treaty provisions.

01

Identity and context

Warm Springs can name both a constituent people and a contemporary confederated tribal government.

Read the sources [1] Confederated Tribes of the Warm Springs Reservation of Oregon

02

A path for deeper reading

Focus the next stage of research on: Distinguish Warm Springs, Wasco and Paiute histories and the confederated government. The sources below are selected reading paths; their authorship, dates and community scope should guide how they are used.

Read the sources [1] Confederated Tribes of the Warm Springs Reservation of Oregon [2] Confederated Tribes of the Warm Springs Reservation of Oregon [3] visit.warmsprings-nsn.gov

03

Constituent histories within a confederation

The government’s history distinguishes Sahaptin-speaking Warm Springs bands, Chinookan-speaking Wasco bands and Paiute communities. It describes different movement and settlement histories before recounting organization of the confederated government in 1937. A shared government does not make these people names interchangeable.

Read the sources [1] Confederated Tribes of the Warm Springs Reservation of Oregon

04

Language education in different settings

The programme describes language learning through schools, daycare and college settings, including Ichishkin and Kiksht. Its public mission is community language education. The page provides an introduction to methods, not assurance that each listed class is currently open or that all learners have the same experience.

Read the sources [2] Confederated Tribes of the Warm Springs Reservation of Oregon

05

A museum for community history

The museum dates its opening to 1993 and describes workshops, archives and a library as parts of public learning. This introduces a community institution alongside the historical narrative. It does not give the Atlas permission to reproduce museum objects, displays or photographs.

Read the sources [4] Museum at Warm Springs / Confederated Tribes of Warm Springs

06

Reading the 1855 agreement carefully

The transcription names different bands and describes land, relocation and promised facilities. Its De Chutes and Columbia references provide historical named-waterway context for the modern river photograph. Neither the written provisions nor the image establishes present boundaries, implementation or ownership.

Read the sources [5] Confederated Tribes of Warm Springs; edited historical treaty transcription

What needs further research

  • Verify current public language/museum access through programme information.
  • Develop more constituent-community voices rather than generalizing one institutional account.
  • Confluence image is modern named-waterway context, not an exact historical settlement or confirmed reservation shoreline.

History — constituent peoples and confederated government ↗

The government distinguishes Wasco, Warm Springs and Paiute histories before explaining reservation change and twentieth-century confederation. A constituent name is not a synonym for all three peoples.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Actual full main historical body read: The Wascoes, The Warm Springs, The Paiutes, Arrival of Settlers, Early Reservation Years, Paiute Settlement and Tribal Government/Indian Self-Determination. Synthesis excludes numeric migration/territory claims.

Review recorded: October 28, 2026

Underlying treaties, constitution, charter and historical records not inspected here. Historical generalizations about livelihoods are scoped to this account, not every family/current identity.

Treaty of 1855 — selected Middle Oregon articles ↗

The community-hosted transcription names distinct bands and sets out reservation, relocation, payment and institutional provisions. Historical wording is not current legal advice or proof of implementation.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Actual preamble and complete Articles1–4 read. Selected band names, De Chutes/Columbia geography, relocation and promised buildings/support. No original manuscript, subsequent statutes or judgments inspected.
